name: Imagination as a way of knowing
description: The claim that the imaginative faculty discovers truth by a route other than argument, and that the poet's invention is a form of perception rather than ornament. Coleridge distinguished primary from secondary imagination and set it against the fancy; Wordsworth made imagination the great agent of moral and intellectual education.

name: Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
description: Landscape treated not as description but as an active influence on thought and feeling: the mountain, the lake, the moor and the wilderness as teachers of the mind, and the external scene as a store of symbols through which inner states become legible.

name: Poetic solitude and the conversation with nature
description: The solitary walker, reaper, or labouring figure whose isolation is not merely social but epistemological: the poem stages a dialogue between one mind and a landscape, moving through dejection toward a recovered capacity for joy.

name: Memory and the growth of the poet's mind
description: The recollected emotion of childhood and early youth as the material of adult poetry, and the long autobiographical poem that traces how a mind was made by places, books, and successive phases of feeling.

name: Revolutionary hope and its disappointment
description: The French Revolution and its wars as the defining political experience of the generation: initial enthusiasm, the Terror and the wars that followed, and the various accommodations—republicanism, radicalism, Tory nationalism, or withdrawn interiority—made by writers who had expected a new age.

name: The supernatural ballad and willed belief
description: Ghostly, demonic, and preternatural agency in narrative verse, together with the deliberate end of that agency: to make readers of an alleged belief feel the interest of the impossible by a traceable human interest and a colour of ordinary life.

name: Gothic confinement and the pursued heroine
description: The sealed castle, convent, labyrinth, and locked chamber as the setting for a young woman pursued by tyrannic male power, with terror, suspense, and the collapse of domestic sanctuary as the plot's engine and its social critique.

name: Sensibility, feeling, and its critics
description: The moral value placed on acute feeling, sympathy, and nervous responsiveness, and the hostile analysis of that value as self-indulgence, theatricality, or danger to judgment—a debate carried on in novels from Mackenzie and Smith to Austen and Peacock.

name: Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
description: The proud, self-exiled, and secretly guilty male figure who defies heaven, law, or society and is defined by that defiance; the mode Byron made European and which shaped protagonists from Manfred to the American outlaw.

name: Idealized love and the lost beloved
description: Love addressed to a figure elevated into a spiritual or Platonic ideal, and the grief, absence, or death that converts desire into meditation; the sequence of sonnets and lyrics that make the beloved's unattainability the subject.

name: Dream, intoxication, and the divided mind
description: Opium, sleep, reverie, and fever as states that split the self and release images beyond the will, with the confessional narrative that tries to account for the pleasure and the ruin they bring.

name: Doubt, faith, and secular questioning
description: Religious belief tested by radical philosophy, biblical criticism, and the apparent silence of nature; prayer and unbelief coexisting in the same poem, and the long argument with a faith inherited but not simply recoverable.

name: Border, ballad, and national memory
description: The old ballad and the border as the preserved memory of a nation: feuds, raids, covenanters, and local legend gathered into print and used to write a national past that could be felt as well as argued.

name: The annual, the keepsake, and the gift-book economy
description: The literary annual and pocket-book as the commercial form of the 1820s and 1830s: steel-engraved plates, presents for ladies, payment to poets by the piece, and the criticism that this made verse a decorative commodity.

name: Exile, travel, and the southern sojourn
description: Voluntary or compelled removal from Britain—to the Continent, to Italy, to Greece, or to America—as a condition of writing: the classics, Catholic culture, and revolutionary politics encountered at first hand, and the homesickness or liberation that follows.

name: Industry, enclosure, and the changed countryside
description: The enclosure of fields, the spread of mills, and the decay of rural labour as poetic subjects: the complaint for a lost common world, the description of machinery and its misery, and the argument about who owns the landscape.

name: Natural history, science, and the poetic eye
description: Geology, botany, chemistry, and anatomy as materials and as threats: the poet who catalogues the local naturalist's world, and the anxiety that a mechanistic or materialist science would dissolve mind, soul, and wonder.

name: The wilderness, settlement, and Indian removal
description: The American forest, lake, and frontier as a stage for race, dispossession, and self-reliance: the vanishing Indigenous presence lamented by settlers whose fiction and guidebooks at the same time justified the advancing boundary line.

name: Republican nationhood and the claim to a national literature
description: The argument that a new republic must produce its own letters rather than import British models, and the institutions—reviews, anthologies, dictionaries, local histories—by which American writing asserted independence of tone and subject.

name: Puritan inheritance and the secret sin
description: Calvinist legacy as a resource for fiction and verse: election, hidden guilt, the watchful community, and the psychological tale in which a concealed transgression works itself out in a New England setting.

name: The marriage market and the limited estate
description: Marriage as an economic arrangement for women with little other provision: entailed property, dependence, reputation, and the narrow field of choice, examined with irony by novelists who made prudence and feeling negotiate.

name: Transatlantic exchange and cultural dependence
description: The circulation of books, reviewers, and imitations between Britain and America: piracy and reprint, the borrowed metre and plot, and the anxiety of a literature measured constantly against the mother country.

name: Early death and the mourning of poets
description: The death of young poets—Keats at twenty-five, Shelley at twenty-nine—as an event that generated elegy, monument, biography, and a lasting argument about whether an early death confirms or destroys a reputation.

name: Familiar prose and the essayist's persona
description: The first-person essay, sketch, and table-talk as a genre that builds a sociable mask for the writer: criticism, reminiscence, and observation blended in a conversational voice addressed to an equal reader.
